index.title: The Top Eigenvalue of Ten Correlated Features
index.prompt: Ten features each have variance 1, and every pair of them has correlation 0.3. Their 10 by 10 covariance matrix C has 1 on the diagonal and 0.3 everywhere else. Without an eigensolver, what fraction of the total variance tr(C) does the largest eigenvalue of C account for?
index.answer: 0.37. Write C = 0.7 I + 0.3 J, where J is the all-ones matrix. J is an outer product, so it has rank 1: its eigenvalues are 10 along (1, ..., 1) and 0 nine times. Then 0.3 J has 3 and nine 0s, and adding 0.7 I adds 0.7 to each: 3.7 once and 0.7 nine times. Check: 3.7 + 9(0.7) = 10 = tr(C). The fraction is 3.7 / 10 = 0.37.

theory.title: Turning One Entry from Real to Repeated to Complex
overview: One entry of a $2 \times 2$ matrix is a dial $c$:

prompt.p: For which value of $c$ do the two eigenvalues of $A$ coincide?

answer.p: The trace is 10 and the determinant is $21 - 2c$, so the characteristic polynomial is
Its two roots are $5 \pm \sqrt{25 - (21 - 2c)} = 5 \pm \sqrt{4 + 2c}$. They coincide when $4 + 2c = 0$, so $c = -2$, and the repeated eigenvalue is 5.

prompt.p: At $c = -2$, find every eigenvector. Can $A$ be written as $V\Lambda V^{-1}$?

answer.p: Both rows say $v_1 + v_2 = 0$, one condition on two unknowns, so the null space is the line through $(1, -1)$ and nothing else. Check: $A(1, -1) = (3 + 2, 2 - 7) = (5, -5)$.

The eigenvectors fill only one line, so no $V$ with two independent eigenvector columns exists, and $A$ cannot be diagonalized. Two independent eigenvectors for the eigenvalue 5 would make $A - 5I$ the zero matrix, so $A = 5I$, and no value of $c$ can change the 2 below the diagonal. Powers of $A$ then pick up a factor of $k$, as the shear's do.

prompt.p: Now set $c = -4$. Find the eigenvalues of $A$ and the largest absolute value $|\lambda|$ among them.

answer.p: The polynomial is $\lambda^2 - 10\lambda + 29$, and $4 + 2c = -4$ is negative, so the roots are $5 \pm \sqrt{-4} = 5 \pm 2i$. No real vector stays on its own line.

For $a + bi$ the absolute value is $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, here $\sqrt{25 + 4} = \sqrt{29} \approx 5.385$ for both. There is a shortcut: the two roots are conjugates, so their product is $|\lambda|^2$, and the product of the eigenvalues is the determinant, $21 - 2c = 29$.

For a recurrent update $\mathbf{h}_t = A\mathbf{h}_{t-1}$ this is the number that matters: complex eigenvalues make the state turn as it goes, by the angle of $5 + 2i$ (about $21.8^\circ$) per step, and $|\lambda| = \sqrt{29} > 1$ makes it grow by that factor per step on average while it turns.

answer.p: Write the start along them: $(0, 1) = (0.75, 0.25) - 0.75\,(1, -1)$. Each day multiplies the first part by 1 and the second by 0.2, so

prompt.p: On which day does $u_n$ first come within $10^{-9}$ of its long-run value?

answer.p: The gap is $0.75 - u_n = 0.75 \cdot 0.2^n$, and it falls below $10^{-9}$ when

So day 13: the gap is $0.75 \cdot 0.2^{12} \approx 3.07 \times 10^{-9}$ on day 12 and $0.75 \cdot 0.2^{13} \approx 6.14 \times 10^{-10}$ on day 13. Stepping the chain would get there too, but only by carrying ten or more decimal places through 13 steps.

The eigenvalue 1 belongs to the split that never changes. The gap shrinks by the other eigenvalue, 0.2, per day, so 0.2 sets how fast the chain forgets where it started. theory.title: The Square Root of a Covariance Matrix

setup.p: a program multiplies vectors of independent standard normal numbers by a symmetric matrix $B$ with $B^2 = S$ and no negative eigenvalues.

prompt.p: Find $B$. What is its off-diagonal entry?

answer.p: Work in the eigenvector basis, where squaring is easy. The eigenvalues of $S$ add up to 122 and multiply to $13 \cdot 109 - 36^2 = 1417 - 1296 = 121$, so they are the roots of $\lambda^2 - 122\lambda + 121 = (\lambda - 121)(\lambda - 1)$. For 121, $S - 121I$ has first row $(-108, 36)$, which says $v_2 = 3v_1$, so $\mathbf{q}_1 = (1, 3)/\sqrt{10}$. Check: $S(1, 3) = (121, 363)$. Since $S$ is symmetric, $\mathbf{q}_2 = (3, -1)/\sqrt{10}$ is perpendicular to it and goes with the eigenvalue 1.

Call the projections onto the two eigenvector lines $P_1 = \mathbf{q}_1\mathbf{q}_1^\top$ and $P_2 = \mathbf{q}_2\mathbf{q}_2^\top$. By the spectral theorem $S = 121P_1 + P_2$. A projection squares to itself, and $P_1P_2 = 0$ because the two lines are perpendicular. So for any numbers $a$ and $b$,

To get $S$ we need $a^2 = 121$ and $b^2 = 1$, and no negative eigenvalues means $a = 11$ and $b = 1$, so $B = 11P_1 + P_2$. In entries, $P_1$ has rows $(0.1, 0.3)$ and $(0.3, 0.9)$, and $P_2 = I - P_1$ has rows $(0.9, -0.3)$ and $(-0.3, 0.1)$, so
Check: $B^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 4 + 9 & 6 + 30 \\ 6 + 30 & 9 + 100 \end{pmatrix} = S$. The off-diagonal entry is 3.

Two shortcuts give wrong answers here. Taking the square root of every entry gives 6 off the diagonal, but squaring a matrix mixes its entries, so that matrix squares to something else. And the diagonal matrix with 11 and 1 has the right eigenvalues but the wrong eigenvectors, $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$: its square has 0 off the diagonal, not 36.

prompt.p: Find every other symmetric matrix whose square is $S$. Would they work for drawing the samples too, and what singles out $B$?

answer.p: Any symmetric matrix with $C^2 = S$ has the same eigenvectors as $S$ here: if $C\mathbf{v} = \mu\mathbf{v}$, then $S\mathbf{v} = \mu^2\mathbf{v}$, and the eigenvalues 121 and 1 of $S$ each have a single line of eigenvectors. So $C$ is $aP_1 + bP_2$ with $a = \pm 11$ and $b = \pm 1$, four matrices in all: $B$, $-B$, and

Any of them squares to $S$, so any of them produces samples with covariance $S$: for a standard normal $\mathbf{z}$, the covariance of $C\mathbf{z}$ is $CC^\top = C^2$. The choice is a convention. The root with eigenvalues 11 and 1 is the one that does not flip any direction, and it is unique, which makes it a well-defined function of $S$, written $S^{1/2}$.

theory.title: How Low the Third Correlation Can Go
overview: Three features are each scaled to mean 0 and variance 1. With the scaled data as the $n \times 3$ matrix $X$, one example per row, their correlation matrix is $C = X^\top X / n$:

setup.p: where $r$ is the correlation of features 2 and 3.

prompt.p: What is the smallest value $r$ can take when $C$ comes from real data?

answer.p: $C$ is $X^\top X$ scaled by $1/n$, which forces it to be PSD: $\mathbf{x}^\top C\mathbf{x} = \lVert X\mathbf{x} \rVert^2 / n \ge 0$. In words, $\mathbf{x}^\top C\mathbf{x}$ is the variance of the combination $x_1 f_1 + x_2 f_2 + x_3 f_3$ of the features, and a variance cannot be negative. Features 2 and 3 both follow feature 1 closely, so try combinations that take them away from it, $\mathbf{x} = (t, -1, -1)$:
This is smallest at $t = 1.8$, where it equals $-3.24 + 2 + 2r = 2r - 1.24$. So $r \ge 0.62$ is needed.

It is also enough. The vector $(0, 1, -1)$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $1 - r \ge 0$. The other two eigenvectors lie in the plane perpendicular to it, spanned by $(1, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 1)/\sqrt2$, where $C$ acts as $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.9\sqrt2 \\ 0.9\sqrt2 & 1 + r \end{pmatrix}$. That block is PSD when its determinant $1 + r - 1.62$ is $\ge 0$, again $r \ge 0.62$. At $r = 0.62$ the eigenvalues are 0, 0.38 and 2.62.

The pairwise range $-1 \le r \le 1$ is far too loose. In angles: the features are vectors, a correlation is the cosine of the angle between two of them, and $\arccos 0.9 \approx 25.8^\circ$. Features 2 and 3 are each within $25.8^\circ$ of feature 1, so they are at most $51.7^\circ$ apart, and $\cos 51.7^\circ \approx 0.62$.

prompt.p: A report built from different subsets of the data lists $r = 0.5$. What is the smallest eigenvalue of this $C$?

answer.p: Use the symmetry between features 2 and 3. The vector $(0, 1, -1)$ is an eigenvector: $C(0, 1, -1) = (0, 1 - r, r - 1) = 0.5\,(0, 1, -1)$, so one eigenvalue is $1 - r = 0.5$.
The other two eigenvectors are perpendicular to it, so they lie in the plane spanned by the unit vectors $\mathbf{e} = (1, 0, 0)$ and $\mathbf{s} = (0, 1, 1)/\sqrt2$. $C$ maps that plane into itself:
So on the plane $C$ acts as $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.9\sqrt2 \\ 0.9\sqrt2 & 1.5 \end{pmatrix}$, with trace 2.5 and determinant $1.5 - 1.62 = -0.12$. Its eigenvalues are

The three eigenvalues add up to $3 = \operatorname{tr} C$, as they should. The negative determinant of the block already shows that one eigenvalue is below 0. Its eigenvector is about $(1, -0.58, -0.58)$, so the combination $f_1 - 0.58 f_2 - 0.58 f_3$ would have a negative variance, which no data can produce. Matrices like this come up when each correlation is estimated from a different set of rows. They cannot be fed to anything that needs a valid covariance, such as sampling from a Gaussian or a Cholesky factorization, until they are repaired.

theory.title: Speeding Up Power Iteration with a Shift
overview: The eigenvalues of a symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix $S$ are 10, 9 and 1, with unit eigenvectors $\mathbf{q}_1$, $\mathbf{q}_2$ and $\mathbf{q}_3$. Power iteration starts from a vector with nonzero parts along all three and rescales to length 1 after each step. Measure its progress by the parts along the eigenvectors that lose, each relative to the part along the one that wins. The slowest of these ratios shrinks by some factor per step: call that factor the rate.

prompt.p: Power iteration on $S$ itself: find the rate. How many steps $k$ does it take until the rate to the power $k$ is below $10^{-6}$?

answer.p: Write the start as $c_1\mathbf{q}_1 + c_2\mathbf{q}_2 + c_3\mathbf{q}_3$. After $k$ steps, before rescaling, it is $10^k c_1\mathbf{q}_1 + 9^k c_2\mathbf{q}_2 + 1^k c_3\mathbf{q}_3$. Rescaling changes all three parts by the same factor, so it does not change their ratios. The winner is $\mathbf{q}_1$. The part along $\mathbf{q}_2$ shrinks relative to it by $9/10$ per step, and the part along $\mathbf{q}_3$ by $1/10$. The slowest of these sets the rate, 0.9.

We need $0.9^k < 10^{-6}$, so $k > 6\ln 10 / \ln(10/9) \approx 131.1$. That is $k = 132$: $0.9^{131} \approx 1.01 \times 10^{-6}$ and $0.9^{132} \approx 9.1 \times 10^{-7}$. Two eigenvalues close together make power iteration slow.

prompt.p: Power iteration can be run on $S - cI$ instead, for a number $c$. Which shift $c$ gives the smallest rate while $\mathbf{q}_1$ still wins? How many steps does it need for $10^{-6}$?

answer.p: If $S\mathbf{q} = \lambda\mathbf{q}$ then $(S - cI)\mathbf{q} = (\lambda - c)\mathbf{q}$, so $S - cI$ has the same eigenvectors with eigenvalues $10 - c$, $9 - c$ and $1 - c$. With $\mathbf{q}_1$ winning, the rate is

For $c \le 5$ the larger of the two is $9 - c$, and the rate $(9 - c)/(10 - c) = 1 - 1/(10 - c)$ falls as $c$ grows. For $c \ge 5$ it is $c - 1$, and the rate $(c - 1)/(10 - c)$ rises as $c$ grows. So the best shift is $c = 5$, where both other eigenvalues have the same size: $S - 5I$ has eigenvalues 5, 4 and $-4$, and the rate is $4/5 = 0.8$.

Then $0.8^k < 10^{-6}$ needs $k > 6\ln 10 / \ln 1.25 \approx 61.9$, so 62 steps instead of 132. The shift moves the competing eigenvalues toward 0 while keeping them smaller than the one we want. A shift past 5 makes $|1 - c|$ the competitor and the rate grows again.

prompt.p: Now take $c = 12$. Which eigenvector of $S$ does power iteration on $S - 12I$ find, and what is the rate?

answer.p: $S - 12I$ has eigenvalues $-2$, $-3$ and $-11$. The largest in absolute value is $-11$, which belongs to $\mathbf{q}_3$, the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue of $S$. So the iteration now finds the bottom eigenvector. The vector flips sign each step, because $-11$ is negative, so compare directions up to sign.

The competitors are $-3$ and $-2$, so the rate is $3/11 \approx 0.273$, much faster than either run above, because the eigenvalue 1 sits far from the other two. This is how power iteration finds the smallest eigenvalue: shift by a number at least as large as $\lambda_{\max}$, so the bottom of the spectrum has the largest absolute value. Here $\lambda_{\min} = -11 + 12 = 1$.

theory.title: The Spectrum of a Similarity Matrix from Three Features
overview: A dataset $X$ has 1000 examples as rows and 3 features as columns, and

setup.p: A kernel method needs the $1000 \times 1000$ similarity matrix $K = XX^\top$, which holds the dot product of examples $i$ and $j$ in row $i$, column $j$.

prompt.p: What is the largest eigenvalue of $K$?

answer.p: The top-left $2 \times 2$ block of $X^\top X$ has characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 6 = (\lambda - 6)(\lambda - 1)$, and the 2 alone on the diagonal is the third eigenvalue. Take an eigenvector, $X^\top X\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ with $\lambda \ne 0$, and multiply both sides by $X$:

$X\mathbf{v}$ is not zero: multiplying $X^\top X\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ on the left by $\mathbf{v}^\top$ gives $\lVert X\mathbf{v} \rVert^2 = \lambda \lVert \mathbf{v} \rVert^2 > 0$. So every nonzero eigenvalue of $X^\top X$ is an eigenvalue of $K$, with eigenvector $X\mathbf{v}$. The argument runs the other way too, so the nonzero eigenvalues of $K$ are exactly 6, 2 and 1. $K$ has rank at most 3, so the other 997 are 0, and the largest is 6.

In SVD terms both matrices are built from $X = U\Sigma V^\top$: $X^\top X = V\Sigma^\top\Sigma V^\top$ and $XX^\top = U\Sigma\Sigma^\top U^\top$, which share the $\sigma_i^2$. A $3 \times 3$ eigenproblem answers a $1000 \times 1000$ one.

prompt.p: What is $\lVert X - X_1 \rVert_F$, where $X_1$ is the best rank-1 approximation of $X$?

answer.p: Each singular value of $X$ is $\sqrt\lambda$ for an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $X^\top X$, so they are $\sqrt6$, $\sqrt2$ and 1. $X_1$ is the first term of the SVD, and by Eckart-Young its Frobenius error is the root of the sum of the dropped $\sigma_i^2$:
Squaring the dropped singular values twice, as if the eigenvalues 2 and 1 were singular values, would give $\sqrt{4 + 1}$, which is the answer to the next part, not this one.

prompt.p: What is $\lVert K - K_1 \rVert_F$, where $K_1$ is the best rank-1 approximation of $K$?

answer.p: $K$ is symmetric and PSD, so its singular values are its eigenvalues, 6, 2, 1 and 997 zeros. (For a symmetric matrix $\sigma_i = |\lambda_i|$, since $K^\top K = K^2$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_i^2$.) Dropping all but the first,

Relative to the whole, the rank-1 version of $K$ keeps more: $\lVert K \rVert_F^2 = 36 + 4 + 1 = 41$, and $36/41 \approx 88\%$ is kept, against $6/9 \approx 67\%$ of $\lVert X \rVert_F^2 = 6 + 2 + 1$ for $X$. Squaring the singular values makes the top one dominate more, so a similarity matrix looks closer to low rank than the data that built it.
